doc.title: Louis Hayes interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 29, 2000

title: Playing style and accompanying in his own voice
summary: Hayes responds to an encyclopedia description of his style, accompaniment as his own voice, and the previous night's solo.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: Well you recorded some marvelous records, you and Woody and I wanted to read a quote that someone wrote about you in one of the jazz encyclopedia type of things, and see if you think this sums you up. It says “Louis Hayes plays in a compelling forceful style marked by a tendency to push the beat and to goad the soloists with frequent fills.”

Yes. I feel great about that, yes. Because I came up in a way where I felt I liked being accompanist but I like doing it on my terms. Because this art form, I always wanted to play it, one of the reasons is because you can accompany a person but you can be your own person, you have your own voice in doing that. So that’s what I really — one of the things I’ve always, I mean the wonderful things about this art form, you can get your own voice, you can have your own voice, and that is one of the main things that you are there for, to do things your own way. So being able to accompany people, I mean soloing was something that I have facilities, and you have to do, being a drummer, is take solos and things. But originally I was thinking about accompanying. That’s the way I started out playing.

Your solo last night in one of the tunes had a great kind of crescendo to it, you know, it sounded like you were playing Bebop rhythms. But by the time you were — you had this impact of almost constant sound. It was like, I don’t know how you were doing it, but it was nice.
Thank you very much. Thank you, Monk.
